content: Obstetric fistula, also known as vaginal fistula, is a serious medical condition characterized by the formation of an abnormal connection (fistula) between the vagina and either the rectum (referred to as rectovaginal fistula) or the bladder (referred to as vesicovaginal fistula). This condition typically arises following prolonged or obstructed labor, particularly in settings where adequate medical care is unavailable. The primary cause of obstetric fistula is prolonged labor, during which the unborn child is compressed so tightly within the birth canal that blood flow to the surrounding tissues is interrupted. This ischemia leads to tissue necrosis, and eventually, the affected tissues deteriorate and form a hole. Less commonly, obstetric fistula can result from female genital mutilation, poorly performed abortions, or pelvic fractures. The clinical presentation of obstetric fistula often includes urinary or fecal incontinence, severe infections, and ulcerations of the vaginal tract. In some cases, nerve damage may lead to paralysis. Beyond the physical symptoms, affected individuals frequently experience profound social stigma due to the persistent odor, perceptions of uncleanliness, and mistaken assumptions of sexually transmitted infections. Additionally, many women with obstetric fistula face infertility, further compounding their social and emotional challenges. Key risk factors for developing obstetric fistula include early pregnancies, closely spaced pregnancies, and lack of access to emergency obstetric care. A study conducted in Nigeria in 1993 revealed that 55% of women with obstetric fistula were under the age of 19, and 94% had delivered their babies at home or in inadequately equipped local clinics. Even when medical interventions such as cesarean sections are available, they are often performed too late, after significant tissue damage has already occurred. The global burden of obstetric fistula is significant. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), an estimated 50,000 to 100,000 women develop obstetric fistulas annually, and over two million women are currently living with fistula-related injuries worldwide.
